data.objective: B2 Use of English: cloze and transformations
data.learn: The Reading and Use of English paper has seven parts in 75 minutes. Parts 1–4 test language in context: multiple-choice cloze, open cloze, word formation and key word transformations. For multiple-choice cloze, compare meaning, grammar and collocation across the whole paragraph. In open cloze, supply one word that fits both sides of the gap. In transformations, use two to five words including the unchanged key word. A familiar expression is not enough: the second sentence must preserve the original meaning.

worked.example: We postponed the trip because it was raining. PUT → We put off the trip because it was raining.
worked.reasoning: “Put off” means postpone. The two-word answer keeps PUT unchanged. “Put away” is grammatical but changes the meaning.

data.objective: B2 Word Formation: building meaning in context
data.learn: In Part 3, the gap needs a form of the supplied word. Read the whole sentence to decide its grammatical role, then check number, negative meaning and spelling. Suffixes are clues, not rules that work for every word. A noun may require a plural ending; an adjective may need a negative prefix. Read the finished paragraph to ensure the meaning fits.

worked.example: The tutor gave a detailed ___ of the method. (EXPLAIN) → explanation. The tutor explained the method ___ . (CLEAR) → clearly.
worked.reasoning: A detailed needs the noun head explanation; explained is already the finite verb, so clearly is an adverb describing how the action was performed. Identify the complete phrase and role before selecting the family form.

data.objective: Tense and aspect: events, duration and evidence
data.learn: Choose tense by the meaning and time relationship, not by a single trigger word. Past simple locates a finished event; present perfect connects an earlier event with now. Past perfect establishes an earlier past event when the sequence needs clarification. Progressive forms describe an activity in progress; many state verbs normally use simple forms. Read the speaker’s viewpoint and the surrounding clauses.

worked.example: When I arrived, the workshop had already started.
worked.reasoning: Arrival is one past event. The workshop began before that event, so past perfect makes the order explicit.

tasks.title: Guided evidence reading: purpose and evidence
tasks.instructions: Read the complete source and answer each question. Use only the evidence given. These are original lesson tasks, not a complete examination paper.
tasks.source:
A library without walls

When Hillford Library began lending books from a converted bus, staff expected most visitors to be older residents who could not reach the town centre. Several did use it, but young families soon became its largest group. The bus stopped beside a playground after school, allowing parents to borrow books while children chose stories together.

The service did not replace the main library. Its small shelves held only a limited selection, so readers ordered specialist titles in advance. Staff brought these on the next visit. This arrangement made the collection feel much larger than the vehicle itself.

The trial also revealed a difficulty: a popular stopping place was beside a busy road. After residents raised safety concerns, the route was changed to use a nearby community centre. tasks.title: Independent passage: purpose and evidence
tasks.instructions: Read the complete source and answer each question. Use only the evidence given. These are original lesson tasks, not a complete examination paper.
tasks.source:
Learning to repair

At nineteen, Mara bought a broken radio from a market because she liked its wooden case. She intended to use it as a decoration, but a neighbour offered to help her repair it. The radio eventually worked, and the experience changed what she noticed when she went shopping. A low price no longer seemed attractive if a product could not be opened without breaking it.

Mara later joined a repair group at college. The sessions were informal, yet safety was taken seriously: volunteers checked plugs before touching any electrical part. Members were encouraged to explain their reasoning rather than take a tool out of a beginner’s hands. This sometimes made a repair slower, but the aim was learning rather than simply increasing the number of fixed objects.

Not everything could be saved. Replacement parts for one printer cost more than a new machine, and another device had been sealed with glue. These failures became useful discussions about product design. Mara does not claim that people should repair every item indefinitely. Some equipment uses so much energy that replacement may be sensible. She believes, however, that buyers should have enough information to make that decision rather than being forced into it by an inaccessible screw or unavailable part.

The group’s approach also changed how Mara responded to mistakes. During her first attempt to mend a lamp, she replaced a part before checking whether it was actually responsible for the fault. A volunteer asked her to explain the evidence for the decision. She realised that she had chosen the most visible component rather than tested the simpler possibilities. The lamp eventually needed only a loose connection secured.

Instead of feeling that the failed attempt had been wasted, Mara began keeping a brief record of what she had checked and why. The notes helped when a similar problem appeared later. They also made it easier to ask for useful advice, because she could explain what had already been tried. She now sees diagnosis as a skill in its own right, rather than a delay before the more satisfying moment of using a tool.

The repair group has considered charging for its work, but members are cautious. A service expected to fix objects quickly might leave less time for explanations. They would prefer a small contribution toward materials while keeping the sessions focused on shared learning. This would not make the group a replacement for a professional repair business. It would give beginners a place to understand ordinary problems and recognise the limits of their knowledge.

tasks.source:
The quiet hour

A supermarket in Longmere introduced a weekly quiet hour after a customer explained that the combination of music, announcements and bright advertising screens made shopping exhausting. Managers turned the music off and stopped non-essential announcements on Tuesday mornings. The lighting remained unchanged because staff needed to read labels and work safely.

Initially, the quiet hour attracted few additional shoppers. A local access group pointed out that the Tuesday timing excluded many people who worked during the day. The supermarket added an early evening session and published the times clearly at the entrance. More customers then used the service.

Some staff expected complaints from other shoppers, but most people barely noticed the absence of background music. Others said the calmer setting helped them concentrate. Managers have not measured whether sales increased, and they avoid presenting the change as a commercial success. The main benefit, in their view, is that customers who previously needed help can shop more independently. Other shops could learn from the trial, but would need to ask their own customers which changes would actually remove barriers.

tasks.title: Independent essay
tasks.instructions: Your class has discussed education. Write an essay: Should colleges offer practical courses alongside traditional subjects? Notes: 1 learning; 2 cost; 3 your own idea. Write 140–190 words.
tasks.model:
Many colleges are deciding whether to provide practical courses as well as traditional subjects. I believe they should offer both, because students need opportunities to connect ideas with real situations.

Practical lessons can make classroom knowledge easier to understand. For example, planning a small garden requires students to calculate area and consider how plants grow. Such activities do not replace mathematics or biology; they give learners a reason to use them carefully.

Cost is a real concern. Workshops need equipment, and schools cannot buy everything. However, sharing tools with a community organisation could make a limited programme affordable. Starting with one project would allow teachers to judge its value before expanding it.

A further advantage is confidence. Students who find written tests difficult may discover that they can solve practical problems successfully. This can encourage them to participate more in other lessons too.

Overall, practical courses deserve a place in education, provided their cost is controlled and their connection with academic learning is clear.

tasks.title: Assessment essay: a new topic
tasks.instructions: Should towns provide more space for teenagers? Notes: 1 leisure; 2 safety; 3 your own idea. Write 140–190 words. Use a clear position and develop all three points.
tasks.model:
Towns should provide more suitable places for teenagers, but young people should help decide what those places offer.

Leisure spaces can give teenagers something positive to do after school. A sports area is useful, yet it will not interest everyone. Rooms for music, art or simply meeting friends would allow more young people to take part.

Safety also matters. A well-maintained centre with approachable staff can be more welcoming than an isolated meeting place. However, supervision should help teenagers feel supported rather than watched constantly. Clear rules agreed with users could achieve this balance.

A further benefit is responsibility. If teenagers help organise events and manage a small budget, they gain practical experience while improving the centre. Adults would still need to offer guidance.

In conclusion, more space would be valuable if it responds to different interests and gives young people a real role. A costly building without suitable activities would be a much weaker investment.

tasks.title: Independent email
tasks.instructions: Your friend Sam may join your college. Write an email explaining an after-class activity, what equipment is needed, and why Sam might enjoy it. Write 140–190 words.
tasks.model:
Hi Sam,

It was great to hear that you are thinking of joining our college. You asked about activities after classes, so I thought I would tell you about the photography club.

We meet on Wednesday afternoons, usually in the media room. The tutor introduces a technique, and then we practise around the campus. Last week we photographed the same scene from different angles, which was much more useful than simply reading camera instructions.

You do not need to buy a camera before joining. The club has a few that members can borrow, although you should reserve one in advance. Comfortable shoes are useful because we sometimes walk quite a long way.

I think you would enjoy the group. Everyone shares ideas, and beginners are welcome. If you arrive before the end of term, come to a session with me and see what you think. I can introduce you to the organiser afterwards.

Let me know when you are coming.

Best wishes,
Alex

tasks.model:
A useful place to study

If you need somewhere to work away from a busy home, the new Riverside Study Centre is worth considering. I spent two afternoons there preparing a group presentation and found it generally well organised.

The main advantage is the choice of spaces. There are quiet desks for individual work and small rooms that groups can book. Our room had a large screen, which made comparing slides much easier. Staff explained the booking system clearly and helped when the connection failed.

There are a few limitations. The café closes early, so anyone working in the evening should bring food. Also, the quiet area can become crowded during examination weeks. Booking ahead is sensible if you need a particular room.

Despite these problems, I would recommend the centre to students who need reliable facilities and a clear separation between discussion and silent study. It is less suitable for someone who wants to work without planning a visit in advance.

tasks.title: Assessment report
tasks.instructions: Your college wants a report about its study area. Describe current strengths, explain two problems, and recommend feasible improvements. Write 140–190 words.
tasks.model:
Report on the college study area

Purpose
This report evaluates the current study area and recommends improvements based on comments from students who use it regularly.

Current strengths
The area is close to teaching rooms and remains open after afternoon classes. Students appreciate the large desks and reliable internet connection. These facilities make it useful for individual assignments and short group meetings.

Problems
The main difficulty is noise. Students discussing projects sit beside people who need to read quietly, so both groups become frustrated. There are also too few power sockets near the central tables. As a result, some students leave when their laptop batteries run low.

Recommendations
I recommend dividing the room into clearly marked discussion and quiet areas. This would require signs and a small change in furniture arrangement rather than major building work. Additional sockets should be considered after an electrical safety check. A short trial followed by student feedback would show whether these changes meet users’ needs.

A shared timetable and a small equipment budget would therefore be necessary. The college should begin with a limited area and review participation before expanding it.

tasks.instructions: Write 80–110 words arguing whether a college should lend laptops. Develop one reason, an example and a condition under which the proposal would work.
tasks.model: A laptop loan scheme could reduce an avoidable barrier to study. Students whose devices fail would still be able to complete assignments instead of missing deadlines while saving for repairs. For example, a short loan during examination week could be more useful than a permanent subsidy for everyone. The college would need clear return dates and technical support, since lending unreliable equipment would simply create a different problem. A small trial could show whether demand justifies a larger scheme. A useful comparison should remain focused on the task, acknowledge uncertainty and give the reader enough detail to understand the proposed action.

tasks.source:
A later start

A college moved one morning workshop from eight to nine after students reported transport difficulties. Attendance improved in the first month, particularly among those travelling from villages. However, the organiser warns that the change coincided with a quieter assessment period. Staff will compare another term before deciding whether the timetable alone explains the improvement. Starting later also means finishing later, which may affect students with afternoon jobs. The college is therefore keeping an alternative early session on one day each week.

answers: The later start is promising, but its effects need further comparison.

tasks.instructions: Read the complete source and answer each question. Use only the evidence given. These are original lesson tasks, not a complete examination paper.
tasks.source:
When a shortcut becomes a destination

The path behind Greystone Station was once used mainly by commuters avoiding the main road. When a local group planted flowers along it, visitors began stopping to look rather than simply walking through. A school added labels describing insects that used the plants, and residents began recording what they saw.

The project did not begin with a detailed wildlife survey. For that reason, the group cannot confidently claim that insect numbers have increased. More sightings may reflect the fact that people are now paying attention. A biology teacher has suggested recording observations at the same time each week to make future comparisons more useful.

The path still needs to function as a route to the station. Some large planters narrowed it too much for wheelchairs and luggage, so they were moved. Volunteers also leave a clear area near the exit to prevent people stopping suddenly in front of commuters.

The project’s value may lie less in a dramatic environmental result than in a changed relationship with an ordinary place. People now notice the seasons and speak with neighbours they previously passed in silence. That is a worthwhile outcome, provided enthusiasm for the garden does not undermine access for those who simply need to catch a train.

questions.evidence: The project did not begin with a detailed wildlife survey.
questions.explanation: The source supports this answer: The project did not begin with a detailed wildlife survey.

questions.prompt: What balance does the station-path account favour?
answers: The project has social value, but environmental claims and access need care.
questions.evidence: The project’s value may lie less in a dramatic environmental result than in a changed relationship with an ordinary place. People now notice the seasons and speak with neighbours they previously passed in silence. questions.explanation: The project has social value, but environmental claims and access need care. Compare the conditions and scope in the passage: the other options remove a stated restriction, confuse measures, or claim more than the evidence establishes.
options: More insect sightings establish that planting increased insect numbers.
The project has social value, but environmental claims and access need care.
The route should become a garden even if commuters cannot pass.
A fixed observation schedule would remove the need to preserve access.

A shared map

Volunteers created a map of public drinking fountains. They initially copied locations from an old council list, but several fountains no longer worked. The group now marks a location as verified only after a recent visit. Users can report a fault, although a volunteer checks the report before changing the map. tasks.title: Independent interview: an urban beekeeper
tasks.instructions: Preview the questions, then play the recording. Listen for the final decision, not simply a repeated word. Replay is allowed in lesson mode. The transcript becomes available after submission.

audio.transcript: Interviewer. What first interested you in keeping bees? Guest. A neighbour invited me to help inspect a hive. I expected to be nervous, but concentrating on the work made me surprisingly calm. I did not decide immediately to keep my own bees. I spent a season helping first, which taught me how much responsibility was involved. Interviewer. Is honey the main reward? Guest. It is enjoyable, but I am more interested in observing how a colony responds to changes in weather and food. People sometimes assume a hive makes any neighbourhood better for wildlife. The situation is more complicated. Managed honeybees can compete with wild insects when flowers are scarce. Planting a wider range of flowers may sometimes help more than adding another hive. Interviewer. What would you advise a beginner? Guest. Find an experienced local group before buying equipment. Books are useful, but conditions vary, and you need someone who can help when a colony behaves unexpectedly. I would also check the rules for the site and speak with neighbours. Being enthusiastic does not remove your responsibility to other people.

audio.transcript: Urban streams are often treated as drains, yet they are also habitats. When rain falls on roofs and roads, water reaches the stream more quickly than it would through soil. This can produce a sudden increase in flow, carrying pollutants and disturbing organisms. One response is to create planted areas that temporarily hold rainwater. These areas slow the movement of water, although their capacity is limited during prolonged storms. Researchers assessing a project should measure both the amount of water retained and how quickly it is released. Counting the number of planted areas alone tells us little about performance. Maintenance also influences results: blocked inlets may prevent water entering a site at all. Finally, a cleaner stream after construction does not prove the planting caused the change. Weather, upstream activity and other improvements may have changed at the same time. Comparing several sites over a longer period gives stronger evidence.

tasks.source:
Measuring the effects of a shorter working week

A small design company introduced a four-day week while keeping salaries unchanged. Managers expected the arrangement to improve retention, but the first evaluation focused mainly on staff-reported fatigue. Employees said they felt less tired and found it easier to manage domestic responsibilities. The report cautioned that these responses did not establish whether productivity had increased.

The company had reduced the length of internal meetings at the same time. Some work that previously required a meeting was handled through written updates. This made it difficult to separate the effect of fewer working days from the effect of a changed communication system. The researchers also noted that most employees worked on projects with flexible deadlines. Results might differ in settings where customers require continuous service.

To improve the next evaluation, the company plans to record missed deadlines, client complaints and staff departures for a full year. It will compare these figures with those from the previous year, while noting any major change in workload. Even this approach cannot control every influence, but it provides more useful evidence than a single satisfaction survey.

The researchers do not argue against shorter working weeks. Instead, they suggest that an appealing policy should be examined with measures that match the claims made for it. Improved wellbeing is valuable in itself; it should not automatically be presented as proof of higher output.

A further difficulty concerns the distinction between output and productivity. Completing the same number of projects in fewer paid hours might suggest greater efficiency, but only if the quality and difficulty of the work remain comparable. If employees complete easier assignments during the trial, a simple project count would overstate the change. Conversely, a team handling a particularly demanding commission might appear less productive despite improving its working methods.

The evaluators therefore proposed describing the work completed as well as counting it. They also wanted to record whether unfinished tasks were being moved into unpaid time. A shorter official week would offer less benefit if employees regularly answered messages on their days off. Staff interviews could reveal this hidden work, although the researchers acknowledged that people may be reluctant to report it. Anonymous responses were suggested as one way to reduce that pressure.

These questions show why evaluating a working arrangement requires more than choosing a favourable headline. Measures should distinguish wellbeing, output, work quality and the distribution of effort. The policy could still be worthwhile if it improves wellbeing without increasing output, provided that its costs are understood and the claim is stated accurately.

tasks.source:
Passage

A public database can appear to be a finished product: users search, download and compare figures without seeing the work that keeps records usable. Yet maintenance often demands as much judgement as initial collection. A change in the definition of a category can make a new figure look comparable with an old one when it is not.

One city discovered this problem when comparing reported cycling journeys across a decade. Earlier surveys counted only travel to work, while later ones included shopping and leisure. The rise in the total therefore reflected both a possible behavioural change and a wider definition. Publishing the numbers without an explanation would have invited a misleading conclusion.

The data team retained the original records and added notes describing each change. It also created a narrower series using only categories shared across the surveys. This made some comparisons possible, although it could not recover information that had never been collected.

Such work is rarely visible in promotional accounts of digital services. A new dashboard may attract attention, while correcting a category description does not. Nevertheless, reliable access depends on both. The writer argues that funding should include long-term documentation and review rather than treating publication as the end of the project. A dataset is useful only when users can understand what its figures represent and where their limits lie.

Researchers’ proposals: A · Lee: retain original records and document changed definitions. B · Rao: remove historical figures whenever definitions change. C · Chen: publish only the latest headline total.

Documentation also needs to explain missing values. A blank entry may mean that no event occurred, that no measurement was taken or that the information could not be released. Treating all blanks as zero would combine fundamentally different situations. The team introduced separate labels for these cases and included examples showing how each should be interpreted.

Version control offered another safeguard. When a record was corrected, the database retained a note of the change rather than silently replacing the figure. This allowed a researcher to understand why an analysis downloaded earlier no longer matched the latest release. Keeping a history did not eliminate errors, but it made them easier to trace and discuss.

There was a cost to this approach. Staff had to decide which explanations were essential and which level of detail would overwhelm ordinary users. The team placed short definitions beside the figures and linked them to fuller notes for specialist readers. This layered presentation recognised that transparency requires communication as well as disclosure. A large archive of technical notes is of limited help if users cannot find the one qualification that changes the meaning of a comparison.

A

Engineers produced a lighter insulation panel and measured its performance in a laboratory. It retained heat effectively under stable conditions. However, buildings experience moisture, vibration and changing temperatures. The team therefore plans field trials before recommending wide adoption. A successful laboratory result establishes potential, not performance in every building.

B

The field trial will compare the panel in occupied homes with different moisture levels. Residents will note any damage, while sensors record indoor temperatures. These observations will help engineers distinguish heat retention from durability: an effective insulator could still be unsuitable if its surface deteriorates quickly.

C

The team will publish the maintenance requirements alongside the thermal results. Buyers should be able to compare the cost of repairs with the energy saved, rather than judge the material only by its weight. The report will state which conditions were tested and which still require investigation.

tasks.source:
When a prediction changes behaviour

A station displayed predicted crowding levels to help passengers choose quieter trains. Some travellers changed departure times, which meant the actual pattern differed from the prediction. The system was not necessarily defective: its information had influenced the behaviour being predicted. Evaluators must therefore consider how people respond to a forecast, rather than treating every difference as a simple error.

tasks.source:
The value of a negative result

Research reports tend to attract attention when a new treatment or method appears to work. A finding that an intervention produced no measurable improvement may seem less newsworthy, yet it can prevent others from repeating an ineffective approach. The absence of an observed effect also needs careful interpretation. A study may be too small, too short or too imprecise to detect a change that exists.

In a trial of classroom lighting, researchers found no clear difference in test performance between two settings. They had measured only one kind of task during a single afternoon. It would therefore be unreasonable to conclude that lighting never affects learning. The result supported a narrower statement: under the tested conditions, this particular change did not produce a detectable difference on that task.

Publishing the method and uncertainty allowed another team to design a longer study. That team could avoid repeating the same limitations and could choose measures more closely related to fatigue. The initial result was therefore useful even without a positive effect.

The writer argues that researchers should describe both what their evidence permits and what remains unresolved. Treating a negative result as failure encourages exaggerated claims and hides useful information. Equally, calling every inconclusive result proof of no effect would be a different mistake. Progress depends on clear questions, transparent methods and conclusions no broader than the evidence supports.

The distinction becomes especially important when results enter public discussion. A headline saying that a method does not work is simpler than an explanation of uncertainty, but it may discourage a useful follow-up study. The opposite headline, claiming that a small unresolved effect proves success, would be equally misleading. Researchers cannot control every summary of their work, yet they can make the limits clear in the report itself.

A well-described negative result can also improve decisions about resources. If several careful studies fail to find the benefit a programme was designed to produce, continuing it unchanged becomes harder to justify. That conclusion depends on the combined evidence, not merely on one unsuccessful afternoon. It may lead to revising the intervention, changing the outcome measured or choosing a different approach.

The writer therefore separates openness to new evidence from a refusal to make decisions. Uncertainty does not mean that all options are equally supported. It means that a decision should reflect the strength of the available evidence and remain open to revision. Publishing methods and results, including those that are disappointing, allows others to understand that judgement and build on it.

tasks.source:
Why a tree count is not enough

City planting programmes often announce how many trees will be added, because a single number is easy to communicate. That total does not show where trees will survive or whom they will benefit. A tree planted beside a pavement without enough soil may remain small, while one in a suitable site can develop a broad canopy.

Researchers comparing neighbourhoods therefore examine canopy cover, species diversity and maintenance as well as planting totals. They also distinguish private gardens from public streets. A leafy district may still have exposed bus stops where people wait in direct sun. The location of shade matters for access, not merely its total area.

Water availability creates another constraint. Species chosen for rapid growth may require more care than a local maintenance team can provide. In one trial, staff recorded survival rates annually and replaced a popular but unsuitable species with a slower-growing alternative. The change reduced the headline planting target but improved the proportion of trees that established successfully.

The writer argues that public reporting should connect targets with outcomes. This does not make tree planting unimportant; it makes its evaluation more useful. A modest programme with suitable sites and reliable care may create more lasting benefit than a larger announcement followed by high losses. The challenge is to communicate this complexity without making the evidence inaccessible to residents.

A distributional question also arises. Two districts with the same average canopy cover may offer very different experiences at street level. In one, shade may be concentrated in private gardens; in another, it may line the routes to schools and shops. A city-wide average can therefore hide whether people can reach useful shade during an ordinary journey. Mapping the location of trees alongside pedestrian routes gives planners a more practical view.

Residents’ knowledge can improve that map. A route that looks shaded from above may still be difficult to use because roots have damaged the pavement or because there are no safe crossings. Consultation does not replace measurement, but it can reveal which measurements are missing. The researchers recommend recording these observations systematically rather than treating them as isolated complaints.

The same reasoning applies to future targets. Announcing an ambitious number of new trees may create political support, yet a programme needs resources for the years after planting. Public reports should show what was planted, what survived and which areas gained usable shade. This would make progress harder to express in one headline, but easier to connect with the reasons the programme exists.

tasks.source:
Learning from a restored wetland

A coastal wetland was restored by reopening channels that had been blocked for agriculture. Water returned quickly, but the vegetation changed more slowly. Early photographs made the project appear complete, while field surveys showed that some expected plant communities had not yet established.

The monitoring team selected several indicators: water levels, plant distribution and the use of the area by birds. These did not always move in the same direction. One bird species became more common while another declined. The team avoided combining every measure into a single success score, because doing so would conceal the different ecological responses.

Local residents also valued the new walking route, although some were concerned about flooding. Engineers explained that the channels were designed for a specific range of tides and that extreme events remained a separate risk. Public meetings helped distinguish the restoration’s intended function from expectations it could not meet.

After five years, the project had created valuable habitat and a well-used public space. Nevertheless, the report describes continuing uncertainty about long-term sediment movement. The writer presents restoration as an ongoing process of observation and adjustment rather than a one-time return to a perfectly known past. This interpretation supports the project while resisting the temptation to declare every outcome settled.

The project also changed how evidence was shared. Early updates used aerial photographs, which clearly showed the reopened channels but revealed little about plant diversity. Later reports combined images with field observations and short explanations of what each indicator could establish. This helped residents see why an area that looked green might still be developing ecologically.

Monitoring involved choices about where and when to collect information. A bird count at one time of day could miss species active at another. The team therefore used a repeatable schedule and recorded unusual weather or disturbance. Consistency made comparisons more useful, although it could not capture every event. The researchers described this as a practical compromise rather than a perfect measure of the wetland.

The report also recorded disagreements about priorities. Some residents favoured easier walking access, while conservation volunteers wanted quiet areas where wildlife would be disturbed less often. The final route avoided several sensitive locations but included viewing points. This did not satisfy every preference, yet it made the trade-off explicit. The writer regards that openness as part of responsible restoration: decisions about a living landscape involve social choices as well as technical evidence.

tasks.title: Independent line-graph report
tasks.instructions: Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
tasks.model:
The line graph compares the proportions of all trips made by bicycle and bus in Norford at four points between 2010 and 2025.

Overall, cycling became more common throughout the period, whereas the share of bus travel declined. Buses accounted for a much larger proportion initially, but bicycles had overtaken them by the final year shown.

In 2010, 10% of trips were made by bicycle, compared with 40% by bus. The cycling figure rose to 15% in 2015 and then increased more rapidly, reaching 25% in 2020 and 35% in 2025. Its overall gain was therefore 25 percentage points.

Bus travel followed the opposite pattern. Its share fell slightly to 38% in 2015, then declined to 35% in 2020 and 30% in 2025. The gap between the two modes narrowed from 30 percentage points at the start to ten in 2020. By 2025, cycling exceeded bus travel by five points. The graph gives proportions rather than total trip numbers.

tasks.title: Assessment: a new bar chart
tasks.instructions: Summarise the new chart. Include an overview and accurate comparisons. Write at least 150 words.
tasks.model:
The bar chart compares average weekly library visits in the North, Central and South districts in 2020 and 2025.

Overall, visits increased in the North and South, while the Central district experienced a small decline. Central remained the busiest of the three in both years, although its lead over North became considerably smaller.

In 2020, Central recorded 400 visits per week, twice the figure for North and well above South’s 150. By 2025, its total had fallen by 20 to 380. This was the only reduction shown in the chart.

North rose from 200 to 320 weekly visits, an increase of 120. South also grew substantially, from 150 to 260, gaining 110 visits. Consequently, the difference between Central and North narrowed from 200 to 60 visits. South remained the least visited district despite its growth, and the gap between North and South changed only slightly, from 50 to 60 visits. The chart does not indicate the reasons for these changes.

tasks.title: Independent pie-chart report
tasks.instructions: Summarise the two pie charts, selecting the main features and making relevant comparisons. Write at least 150 words.
tasks.model:
The pie charts show how household electricity use was divided among four categories in 2015 and 2025.

Overall, appliances replaced heating as the largest category. The proportions used for heating and lighting fell, while appliances and other uses both gained share. The charts do not show whether total electricity consumption increased or decreased.

In 2015, heating accounted for 40% of electricity use, making it the largest category. Appliances followed at 30%, while lighting represented 20% and other uses the remaining 10%. Together, heating and appliances therefore made up 70% of the total.

By 2025, the appliance share had risen by ten percentage points to 40%. Heating had fallen by the same amount to 30%, so the combined proportion of these two categories remained unchanged. Lighting’s share halved to 10%, whereas other uses doubled to 20%. Although these changes altered the distribution, the absence of total consumption figures means that a smaller percentage cannot automatically be interpreted as a smaller amount of electricity.

tasks.instructions: Describe the process, including its overall sequence and the rejection branch. Write at least 150 words.
tasks.model:
The diagram illustrates how used paper is processed into new paper.

Overall, the process consists of a sequence beginning with collection and ending with finished paper being rolled. Unsuitable material is removed during sorting, while the accepted paper continues through several treatment and drying stages.

First, used paper is collected and taken to be sorted. At this point, rejected material leaves the main process. The paper that is retained is then mixed with water. This mixture passes through a filtering stage before it is pressed.

After pressing, the material is dried. The dried paper is finally formed into rolls, which are the output shown at the end of the diagram. All the main stages proceed in one direction, and the diagram does not show any material returning to an earlier step. It also provides no information about the time required, the temperature used for drying or the quantity of paper produced. These details therefore cannot be included as factual parts of the description.

tasks.title: Independent full Task 2
tasks.instructions: Some people think public libraries should focus only on printed books. Others believe they should also provide digital services. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
tasks.model:
Public libraries are sometimes judged mainly by how many printed books they lend. In my view, they should continue to provide books while also offering practical access to digital services. The purpose is to help people obtain and use information, and that purpose does not depend on one medium.

Printed books remain valuable because they can be read without a device or internet connection. A local collection also gives readers access to material they may not be able to buy. For children, choosing books with a knowledgeable librarian can make reading less intimidating and encourage interests that an online recommendation system might not reveal.

At the same time, digital support meets a different need. Applications for work, housing and public services often require online forms. Providing computers without guidance may be insufficient for someone who has little experience using them. A short appointment with trained staff can help users complete a task independently rather than leaving them dependent on relatives.

There is a reasonable concern about resources. Staff time and equipment are limited, so every new service has an opportunity cost. Libraries should therefore consult users and review demand instead of adding technology simply because it appears modern. Partnerships with local organisations may also provide specialist training without requiring librarians to solve every technical problem.

Overall, books and digital support serve related educational and social purposes. A balanced library should preserve a useful collection while responding to genuine barriers to information. Its success should be assessed through the quality and accessibility of those services, rather than through a single measure such as book loans or computer numbers.

tasks.title: Assessment: opinion essay
tasks.instructions: Some people believe that public spaces should be designed mainly for organised events. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Write at least 250 words.
tasks.model:
Public spaces can support organised events, but I disagree that this should be their main purpose. Their greatest value is often that people can use them freely in ordinary life, including when no programme has been arranged.

Events can bring people together and give local businesses opportunities. A concert or market may introduce residents to activities they would not otherwise encounter. However, a space designed primarily for large gatherings may offer little comfort on a quiet weekday. Broad paved areas can accommodate crowds while leaving few places to sit in shade or talk without interruption.

Everyday access serves a wider range of needs. A parent may need somewhere to pause with a child, an older person may value a short walk with regular seating, and a worker may simply want to eat lunch outdoors. These uses do not produce impressive attendance figures, but they contribute to the quality of daily life. They also require attention to practical details such as accessible paths, maintenance and toilets.

A flexible design can support both purposes. Movable furniture and a modest open area may allow occasional events without removing gardens or quiet corners. Organisers should also consider noise and the periods when public access is restricted. A popular festival does not justify making the space unavailable to residents for much of the year.

In conclusion, organised activities are a useful part of a public space’s role, but they should complement rather than dominate everyday use. Design should begin with the varied needs of ordinary users and accommodate events where they fit. This would make the space valuable beyond the moments when it attracts a large crowd.

tasks.title: Independent full Task 2
tasks.instructions: Traffic congestion is increasing in many cities. What are the main causes, and what measures could address them? Write at least 250 words.
tasks.model:
Many cities face increasing traffic congestion, and it is tempting to seek one simple solution. In my view, improving public transport and managing road demand need to work together. Either approach alone may shift the problem rather than solve it.

A major cause of congestion is that many journeys are difficult to make without a car. Housing and employment may be separated by long distances, while bus routes fail to connect the places people actually need to reach. A person cannot reasonably be expected to abandon driving if the alternative involves an unreliable service and several changes. More frequent routes and clear connections can therefore make shared transport a realistic choice.

However, additional buses will not automatically reduce traffic if driving remains the easiest option for every trip. Cities may need to limit parking in crowded areas or charge for scarce road space. Such measures can discourage unnecessary car journeys, but they must be introduced carefully. Workers travelling at unusual hours and people with mobility needs may have fewer alternatives than office commuters.

An effective policy would combine better services with targeted demand management. Revenue from parking charges, for example, could help fund routes serving areas that currently have poor access. Authorities should also publish evidence about reliability, journey times and the distribution of costs. This would allow residents to judge whether the policy is meeting its stated goals.

In conclusion, congestion reflects both transport provision and the incentives affecting individual choices. Coordinated improvements offer a stronger response than expecting one new road or one charge to transform travel. The aim should be accessible movement, with fair options for people whose needs differ.

tasks.title: Assessment: full two-part essay
tasks.instructions: Why might residents hesitate to use a new public service, and what can organisers do to encourage appropriate participation? Answer both questions. Write at least 250 words.
tasks.model:
A new public service can attract fewer users than its organisers expect, even when it addresses a real need. Hesitation may arise from practical barriers, unclear information or uncertainty about whether the service is intended for a particular person. Encouraging participation therefore requires more than wider advertising.

One reason is that potential users cannot easily judge what will happen when they attend. A notice may name an advice session without explaining whether appointments are needed, what documents to bring or whether there is a charge. People who have had a discouraging experience elsewhere may be especially reluctant to risk an unnecessary journey. Others may understand the offer but be unable to attend at the advertised time.

Organisers should first investigate these different barriers. Speaking only to current users may produce a positive picture while missing the people who never arrive. Short conversations with non-users, conducted through trusted local groups, can reveal whether the main difficulty is information, access or the service itself. The questions should invite criticism rather than assume that reluctance reflects a lack of interest.

The response can then be specific. Clear examples of who the service can help, practical booking instructions and a low-commitment introductory session may reduce uncertainty. Different opening times or an accessible alternative may address physical and scheduling barriers. However, encouraging everyone to attend regardless of need could overload the service, so communication should also explain its limits and direct people elsewhere when appropriate.

Overall, hesitation is often understandable rather than irrational. Organisers can encourage suitable participation by explaining the complete experience, consulting missing voices and changing practical arrangements where evidence shows a barrier. Success should mean useful access for the intended users, not simply a larger attendance total.

Although the pattern suggests continued growth, the figures do not explain its causes or establish that the projection will be achieved. A report should therefore distinguish the two measured points from the expected future total.

tasks.title: Independent full advantages/disadvantages essay
tasks.instructions: Technology increasingly allows people to work from home. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages? Write at least 250 words.
tasks.model:
Technology has made home working possible for many occupations, and I believe its advantages can outweigh its disadvantages when organisations manage it carefully. The benefit is flexibility rather than the assumption that every job should become remote.

A major advantage is the reduction in unnecessary travel. Workers can use time previously spent commuting for rest, family responsibilities or focused work. Employers may also recruit people who live farther away or have difficulty attending an office every day. These gains can widen access to employment, provided the role can genuinely be performed remotely and the worker has suitable equipment.

The disadvantages concern both working conditions and communication. A home may lack a quiet space, and the boundary between work and personal time can become unclear. Employees may feel expected to answer messages throughout the evening. Informal learning is also harder when beginners cannot easily observe experienced colleagues or ask a brief question. These problems would make unrestricted remote working unsuitable as a universal rule.

However, they can be reduced through clear arrangements. Employers should define availability, provide appropriate support and create deliberate opportunities for collaboration. Some teams may benefit from a hybrid pattern, while others can work remotely with scheduled contact. The decision should reflect the task and the employee’s circumstances rather than a desire to treat every worker identically.

In conclusion, technology-enabled home working offers substantial advantages in time and access, but those benefits depend on reasonable boundaries and effective communication. I therefore favour it as a supported option rather than a compulsory replacement for workplaces. Under those conditions, the flexibility it creates is likely to be more valuable than the difficulties it introduces.

data.learn: Prepositions express relationships: increase by gives a change, increase to gives an endpoint, and rise from introduces a starting point. tasks.model: The rate increased from 5% to 8%, a rise of three percentage points. This describes the proportion affected, not necessarily the number of people. If the underlying population changed, the absolute count might follow a different pattern. The figures therefore support a statement about the rate but do not establish how many additional individuals were involved. They also provide no explanation for the change. A careful report should preserve these distinctions rather than replacing the percentages with an unsupported claim about total cases.

tasks.title: Independent response
tasks.instructions: Describe a skill you learned from another person. Say what it was, who helped, how you learned, and why it mattered. Prepare for one minute, then speak for up to two minutes.
tasks.model:
A practical skill I learned from another person was repairing a punctured bicycle tyre. My neighbour, Helen, taught me about two years ago, shortly after I started cycling to work. I had been paying a shop to fix every puncture, so I wanted to handle a simple repair myself rather than stop cycling whenever something went wrong.

We worked in her garden on a Saturday morning. First she showed me how to remove the wheel and find the hole in the inner tube using a bowl of water. Instead of doing everything for me, she asked what I thought the bubbles meant. That small question helped me understand the reason for each step, rather than just memorise a sequence.

The awkward part was putting the tyre back. I trapped a section of the tube under the edge, and Helen noticed before I inflated it. We took it off again, checked the position and tried a second time. I felt slightly embarrassed, but she explained that checking a mistake was part of learning a safe repair.

Later that month I had another puncture on the way home. It took me longer than it would have taken a mechanic, but I managed it. The lesson mattered because it gave me useful independence and changed how I ask for help. I now prefer someone to explain a decision and let me try it, instead of taking over immediately.

I also remember how patient Helen was when I asked the same question twice. She suggested keeping a small repair kit in my bag, but reminded me that some problems still need professional attention. That distinction was useful: being independent did not mean pretending to know everything. It meant recognising a repair I could attempt safely and knowing when to stop.

tasks.title: Independent response
tasks.instructions: Describe a time you solved a problem with other people. Say what the problem was, who helped, what you did and how you felt. Prepare for one minute, then speak for up to two minutes.
tasks.model:
One occasion when I solved a problem with other people was the opening of our college exhibition last spring. Four of us had spent several weeks arranging photographs in different rooms. We had checked the display boards and lighting, but we had forgotten to test the route from the main entrance.

Just before the opening, a visitor asked where the exhibition was. We realised that the corridor split in two and there were no signs. Simply telling that visitor would not solve the problem for the next fifty people, so we stopped and divided the work. I drew a quick plan, two classmates made large arrows, and another waited by the entrance while we put them up.

There was a small disagreement about whether the signs needed to look professional. One classmate wanted to print them, but the nearest printer was in another building. We agreed that clear temporary signs were more useful than perfect ones arriving late. We used thick pens and placed each arrow where a visitor actually had to choose a direction.

Ten minutes later we walked the route ourselves. One arrow was partly hidden by a door, so we moved it. After that, people found the rooms without asking for help. I felt relieved, but also pleased that we had listened to each other under pressure. The experience taught me to check an event from a visitor's point of view, and to decide which part of a problem needs attention first.

After the exhibition we added a visitor walk-through to our planning checklist. It was a simple change, but it gave everyone a chance to notice problems that the organisers had become used to. I would use the same approach again: agree on the immediate goal, share the jobs and then test the solution instead of assuming that putting up a sign has finished the task.

audio.transcript: Today we will look at how plants respond to limited water. One visible response is wilting, but important changes may occur before leaves lose their shape. Some plants close tiny openings on their leaves, reducing water loss. Those openings also allow gases to move in and out, so closing them can restrict the carbon dioxide available for photosynthesis. The response therefore involves a trade-off rather than a cost-free solution. Researchers comparing species must consider when and where they grow. A plant adapted to brief dry periods may respond differently from one that regularly faces long droughts. In an experiment, giving all plants the same amount of water does not necessarily create the same degree of stress, because leaf area and root systems vary. Measurements should match the question being asked. If we want to understand survival, a short-term change in growth is relevant but not sufficient on its own.

tasks.source:
How social learning can preserve a mistake

Animals can learn by observing others, which may save time and reduce the risks of exploring unfamiliar food or places. However, copying is useful only when the observed behaviour suits the current situation. A route that once led to food may no longer do so after conditions change.

In one experimental design, researchers allow a few individuals to discover a feeding location and then introduce inexperienced animals. If the newcomers follow the experienced group, this shows that social information influences their choice. It does not establish that the copied choice is always the best one. To test flexibility, the researchers can move the food and observe whether individuals continue following the old route.

Persistence may look like an inability to learn, but its interpretation depends on the cost of exploration. When searching independently is dangerous, following a usually reliable group may remain a reasonable strategy even after occasional failure. The important question is how animals balance personal experience with social information.

This distinction also affects how the findings are described. Saying that animals “blindly copy” may exaggerate what a limited experiment demonstrates. A more careful account identifies the conditions under which copying continues and the evidence that causes behaviour to change. Social learning is neither an infallible solution nor a simple error; its value depends on the environment and the alternatives available.

tasks.source:
A measurement that changed its meaning

A research group compared household energy use over several years. At first, the figures appeared to show a sharp increase. The team then discovered that the recording system had changed: earlier records included only purchased electricity, while later ones also estimated energy generated by household solar panels.

The apparent rise therefore combined a possible change in behaviour with a broader measurement definition. The researchers reconstructed a narrower series using the categories shared across the records. This reduced the size of the increase but did not remove it entirely. They described the revised pattern as evidence of a moderate rise, while noting that some historical information remained unavailable.

The case illustrates why a word such as “consumption” needs an operational definition. A familiar label does not guarantee that every dataset measures the same thing. Comparisons are useful when differences in collection and classification are understood. Without that context, greater numerical detail may create an illusion of precision rather than a more reliable conclusion.

tasks.source:
When a health average hides variation

An average can summarise a health outcome, but it may conceal important differences among participants. Suppose a programme produces a modest average improvement while helping one group substantially and making little difference to another. Reporting only the overall figure would not show who benefited or why.

Researchers therefore examine variation, while avoiding the temptation to explain every subgroup difference after seeing the results. Dividing a small sample into many categories can produce apparent patterns by chance. A useful analysis distinguishes questions planned in advance from exploratory observations that need confirmation.

The way an outcome is measured matters too. A self-reported improvement in comfort is valuable, but it is not identical to a change in physical function. Neither measure should automatically replace the other. Together, they may provide a fuller account of what participants experience.

The writer argues for reporting benefits with enough detail to reveal uncertainty and practical meaning. This does not make an intervention ineffective simply because its effects vary. It helps readers understand which claims are supported and what further research should investigate.

tasks.title: Independent Academic Discussion
tasks.instructions: Professor: Should colleges require a community project as part of every course? Lina says projects make learning meaningful. Omar worries about time and scheduling. Contribute your own view, respond to an idea in the discussion, and develop your reasoning. Aim for at least 100 words in this ten-minute local practice.
tasks.model: I agree with Lina that community projects can make learning more meaningful, but I would prioritise a clear connection with the course. A project that merely keeps students busy may use time without helping them understand the subject. For example, a biology class could compare plant growth in two local gardens and explain the limits of its observations. Students would practise collecting evidence while producing something useful for residents. Omar’s concern about scheduling is reasonable, so participation should be planned within teaching time rather than relying entirely on evenings. A small, focused project would be more manageable than a large event and would make its educational value easier to evaluate.

tasks.instructions: Professor: Our university can fund either a peer-mentoring scheme for first-year students or additional drop-in advice sessions with staff. Lina favours mentors because students share practical experience. Omar prefers staff because advice must be accurate. Contribute your view, engage with at least one student, and support your position. Aim for at least 100 words.
tasks.model: I would give priority to peer mentoring, but with staff support for questions that require specialist advice. Lina makes a useful point about shared experience: a student who has recently adjusted to university can explain everyday routines in a way a formal information sheet may not. For example, a mentor could show a new student how to organise group work or find a quiet study space. Omar is right that accuracy matters, especially for course rules or financial decisions. Mentors should therefore have clear guidance about when to refer someone to staff. This arrangement would widen informal support without asking students to replace professional advisers. A small pilot could also reveal which questions most often need referral.

tasks.instructions: Professor: A university is considering replacing some large lectures with small workshops. Sara believes workshops make participation easier. Ben worries that fewer lectures would reduce access to expert explanations. What arrangement would you recommend? Engage with a viewpoint and explain your reasoning. Aim for at least 100 words.
tasks.model: I would retain a shorter expert lecture and use the remaining time for small workshops. Sara is right that students need opportunities to test their understanding rather than only listen. In a workshop, they could explain an answer to a partner and discover which step they have misunderstood. However, Ben identifies a real risk: students may struggle if they are asked to solve problems before the key concepts have been explained. A short lecture could introduce those concepts, while a prepared workshop task would require students to apply them. Tutors could collect common difficulties and pass them back to the lecturer. This would connect explanation and participation rather than make them competing priorities.

audio.transcript: When organisations measure service quality, they often begin with satisfaction surveys. These can reveal useful experiences, but their interpretation depends on who responds. People who complete a service successfully may be more willing to answer than those who abandoned it. A high satisfaction figure can therefore coexist with serious access problems. One way to investigate this is to record where users leave a process and ask a sample of non-completers about the difficulty. The aim is not to dismiss positive feedback, but to place it alongside evidence from people whose experience is less visible. Evaluators should also distinguish a polite interaction from a successful outcome. A staff member may be helpful even when the procedure prevents a person from obtaining what they need.

Who benefits from a redesigned high street?

A high street redesign is often presented as a choice between cars and pedestrians. That framing overlooks how many different journeys a street supports. A delivery driver, a wheelchair user, a parent with a pushchair and a shop assistant travelling home late may all need different things from the same space.

The recent proposal for Westbridge removes some parking to widen pavements and add seating. Those changes could make the street more comfortable, especially where narrow paths currently force people to move into the road. However, the proposal says little about deliveries or access after public transport becomes less frequent in the evening. These omissions deserve attention before construction begins.

This is not an argument for preserving every parking space. A street is a shared public place, and storing private vehicles should not automatically take priority over safe movement. Equally, a design described as accessible should be tested with people who face practical barriers, rather than judged only from an attractive drawing.

I would support a temporary trial using movable planters and marked loading areas. Residents and businesses could then report specific difficulties while the layout is still easy to adjust. The council should publish what it learns, including problems that do not fit the original expectations. A successful project would improve everyday access for a wider range of people, not merely produce a more impressive photograph of the town centre.

The changing life of a public building

The old market hall in Alderwick has served several purposes since trading moved elsewhere. It was used for storage, stood empty for years and later became a venue for occasional events. Each phase left traces in the building, from repaired doorways to marks showing where temporary partitions had stood.

A current proposal would turn it into a community workshop and exhibition space. Supporters describe this as a return to the hall’s original role as a meeting place. The phrase is appealing, but the building’s history is less simple. Trading brought people together, yet access and influence were not shared equally. A new public use should therefore be judged by present needs rather than by an idealised account of the past.

The survey has identified practical questions. The roof needs repairs, and the main entrance includes steps. An accessible entrance could be created on the east side, but this would affect the layout of one proposed workshop. Organisers also need a realistic plan for heating and staffing during quieter months.

None of these issues means the project should be abandoned. They show why a useful feasibility study must go beyond an attractive picture of a finished building. A phased approach could begin with a safe, accessible section and expand once demand is clearer. The hall’s history offers possibilities, not a guarantee that every proposed activity will succeed.

A phased plan also has risks. An unfinished appearance could make residents doubt whether the project will ever be completed, while repeated building work may disrupt early users. Organisers propose publishing a sequence of achievable stages, with a clear explanation of what each stage would provide. This would allow the public to distinguish a limited first opening from a promise that every proposed facility is already available.

Consultation has revealed differences in expected use. Some residents want classes led by qualified tutors, while others mainly need affordable space for groups they organise themselves. Both could fit the building, but they imply different staffing and booking arrangements. The project team has therefore resisted treating a large number of expressions of interest as proof of one uniform demand. It will ask what people would attend, when they could come and what they could reasonably pay.

These practical questions connect the building’s history with its future without pretending that the past supplies a complete answer. Preserving a market hall can protect a distinctive part of the town, but preservation should enable useful access rather than turn the building into a symbol that residents cannot afford to use. The writer’s support remains conditional on a plan that explains both its ambitions and its limits.

Choosing a practical course

Three evening courses are available at the adult learning centre. The bicycle-maintenance course runs on Mondays and supplies tools, but participants should bring a bicycle if possible. The cooking course meets on Wednesdays and requires learners to disclose allergies before enrolment. Ingredients are included in the fee. The digital-skills course runs on Thursdays; laptops are supplied, although learners may use their own device.

All courses require advance booking. Places are confirmed only after payment, and a waiting-list request is not a confirmed place. Refunds are available until seven days before the first session. After that point, a transfer to another person may be possible if the organiser agrees. The centre cannot guarantee a transfer when a course has specific entry requirements.

Learners who need an accessible room or communication support should contact the centre before booking. Staff will discuss arrangements rather than assume that one standard adjustment suits every person. The programme offers useful opportunities, provided applicants read the conditions and choose a course that matches their needs.

tasks.source:
Training that transfers to work

A retailer introduced short customer-service workshops after staff reported uncertainty about handling unusual requests. The sessions used examples drawn from the shop rather than a list of memorised phrases. Participants discussed what the customer needed, which rules applied and when a supervisor should be involved.

An initial survey found that staff felt more confident. The training team welcomed this response but recognised that confidence did not establish better performance. Supervisors therefore observed a sample of interactions and recorded whether staff identified the issue, explained options clearly and followed the relevant procedure.

Some employees improved quickly, while others needed practice with specific situations. The team used these differences to plan follow-up sessions rather than ranking staff from a single observation. It also revised a rule that had caused confusion even among experienced employees.

The account suggests that effective training connects explanation, realistic practice and feedback. It does not claim that one workshop can solve every service problem. Some difficulties arise from unclear procedures or inadequate staffing, and asking employees to speak more confidently would not address those causes.

tasks.source:
Why a pilot can be informative without being decisive

A local employer tested a quieter break room after staff requested somewhere away from the main canteen. The room was used regularly, and several workers reported feeling more rested. The pilot therefore showed demand for a different kind of space.

It did not establish that the room reduced sick leave. Absence figures changed during the trial, but shift patterns and staffing levels also changed. A small number of cases could strongly affect the total. The evaluation separated the direct evidence of use from the more uncertain claim about health outcomes.

The employer decided to retain the room while collecting longer-term feedback. This was a practical decision based on a modest cost and a clearly expressed need. It did not require pretending that every possible benefit had already been proved.

The writer argues that evidence should match the scale of a decision. A low-cost reversible change may be reasonable on limited evidence, while a large permanent investment requires more. The important point is to describe the basis of the decision honestly and remain willing to adjust it.

tasks.source:
A town connected to distant markets

When a small food producer began selling online, orders arrived from places the owner had never visited. The wider market allowed the business to grow, but it also changed the work. Packaging, delivery enquiries and returns took time that had previously been spent making products.

The owner first assumed that more orders would always improve profitability. After reviewing costs, she found that a few distant deliveries generated little income once breakages and staff time were included. She limited delivery to areas where reliable services were available and explained the restriction clearly to customers.

This decision was not a rejection of wider trade. It was an attempt to make growth sustainable for a small team. Local sales remained important because customers could collect purchases and discuss products directly. Online orders offered a different benefit by smoothing demand beyond the busiest market days.

The writer sees the example as a reminder that global connections create both opportunities and responsibilities. The useful question is not whether a business is local or international, but whether its arrangements support the people doing the work and deliver what customers are promised.

tasks.source:
The return of a neighbourhood workshop

The workshop on Milton Road began as a place where residents could borrow tools. Its organisers soon discovered that access to equipment was only one part of the need. Some members did not know which tool suited a task, while others were confident using it but uncertain about safety checks.

The group introduced short demonstrations and a system allowing beginners to work beside experienced volunteers. This slowed some sessions, yet it made the workshop more welcoming. Members were encouraged to explain what they were trying to achieve before choosing equipment, which sometimes revealed that a simpler method would be safer.

As attendance grew, the organisers faced pressure to open more often. They resisted an immediate expansion because a few volunteers were already carrying most of the responsibility. A survey asked members which additional session would be most useful and whether they could contribute time. The resulting rota added one evening without requiring the same people to supervise every week.

The workshop also kept a record of repairs that could not be completed. These failures helped identify missing skills and unavailable parts. They were not removed from the annual report simply to make the project appear more successful.

The writer argues that a community service develops through careful attention to limits as well as enthusiasm. The workshop’s value lies in shared knowledge and practical access, but maintaining that value requires training, realistic staffing and honest reporting. A larger programme would not necessarily be a better one if it exhausted the people keeping it open.

An additional debate concerned membership fees. Some volunteers argued that a higher fee would provide stable income and reduce the need to apply for small grants. Others worried that the people most likely to benefit from borrowing equipment might be the least able to pay. The group introduced a standard fee with a confidential reduced-rate option, while continuing to seek support for training. This did not remove the financial uncertainty, but it made the trade-off visible.

The organisers were also careful about the language of independence. Their aim was not to suggest that every resident should become an expert or that asking for professional help represented failure. Some repairs require specialist knowledge, and knowing when to stop can be as valuable as learning a new technique. A notice beside the workbench explained which jobs the volunteers could support and which should be referred elsewhere.

Looking ahead, the group plans to review who uses the workshop as well as how often it opens. If attendance grows mainly among already confident members, a larger timetable may not improve access for beginners. The next evaluation will therefore include short conversations with people who joined once and did not return. Their experience could reveal barriers that regular users no longer notice. Expansion remains possible, but it will follow evidence about need and capacity rather than become a measure of success in itself.

tasks.title: Guided formal letter
tasks.instructions: Your rented flat has no heating. Write to the property agency: explain the problem, describe its effect, and request action. First identify the three points, then write at least 150 words. Use a suitable opening and closing.
tasks.model:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing about the heating in the flat I rent at 18 Willow Street. The system stopped working on Monday evening, and the problem has continued despite my attempts to reset the thermostat according to the instructions provided.

The flat is particularly cold in the morning, which makes it difficult to work from home. I am also concerned that the problem may worsen if it is left unchecked. I have not attempted any repair myself because the equipment should be examined by a qualified engineer.

Could you arrange an inspection as soon as possible and confirm the expected visit time? I am available before ten on Thursday or throughout Friday. If an earlier appointment is possible, please contact me so that I can make arrangements. I would also appreciate advice about a safe temporary heating option while the system is unavailable.

Please let me know what action will be taken and when I can expect an update.

Yours faithfully,
Maya Karim

data.objective: General Training Task 2: developing a complex position
data.learn: A nuanced argument answers the question clearly while recognising relevant conditions. Complexity comes from explaining relationships, not from avoiding a position. tasks.title: Guided position paragraph
tasks.instructions: Write 60–90 words distinguishing training required for a current job from training for a different career. Explain why the distinction matters.
tasks.model: Training required for a current job should normally be supported by the employer, because the organisation decides which equipment and procedures workers must use. A course intended mainly for a different career has a less direct connection with that responsibility. This does not mean employees should receive no help with wider development, but it suggests that funding decisions should consider the purpose and expected benefit rather than applying one rule to every course.
