tasks.title: Independent full Task 2
tasks.instructions: Some people believe employers should provide all work-related training. Others think employees should manage their own development. Discuss both views and give your opinion. Write at least 250 words.
tasks.model:
Some people argue that employers should provide training whenever workers need new skills, while others believe employees should take responsibility for their own development. I think responsibility should be shared, with the balance depending on who benefits and whether the training is required for the job.

Employers should normally provide instruction that workers need to perform their current duties safely and effectively. If a company introduces new equipment, it controls both the decision and the working conditions. Expecting employees to learn alone could lead to inconsistent practice and avoidable mistakes. Paid training time also makes participation possible for workers who have caring responsibilities or limited resources outside work.

Employees nevertheless have a role in identifying their learning needs and using opportunities actively. A course will achieve little if participants do not practise or ask about difficulties. Workers may also choose to develop skills for a different career, and it would be unreasonable to expect their present employer to fund every personal ambition. In those cases, public education or individual study may be more appropriate.

A practical arrangement would begin with a discussion of the skill required, the expected benefit and the support needed. The employer could provide time and essential resources, while the employee agrees on a realistic learning plan and applies the new skill. Progress should be reviewed through actual work rather than attendance alone.

In conclusion, neither complete employer responsibility nor complete individual responsibility is convincing. Training linked directly to current work should be supported by the organisation, while employees should participate thoughtfully and take initiative. Clear agreements are more useful than broad claims that one side must bear every cost.

tasks.title: Guided argument analysis
tasks.instructions: Write 60–90 words explaining why repeated local activities might support social connections more effectively than one large event. Include a limitation.
tasks.model: Repeated activities give people time to recognise one another and develop trust. A weekly repair group, for example, allows neighbours to exchange practical help over several months rather than meet only once. However, regular meetings can exclude people whose schedules vary, so organisers should consider different times and ways to participate. The benefit comes from meaningful repeated contact, not simply from counting how many sessions appear on a calendar.

tasks.title: Independent full essay
tasks.instructions: Some people think local councils should spend more on large cultural events. Others prefer regular neighbourhood activities. Discuss both views and give your opinion. Write at least 250 words.
tasks.model:
Some towns spend large sums on major cultural events, while smaller neighbourhood activities receive less attention. I believe both can have value, but local authorities should give priority to activities that residents can use regularly and that remain affordable to maintain.

A large festival can attract visitors and create opportunities for local businesses. It may also bring residents together around a shared experience. These benefits are strongest when local people can participate rather than simply watch an event designed mainly for tourists. However, a brief increase in visitor numbers does not establish a lasting improvement in community life.

Regular neighbourhood activities offer a different advantage. A weekly repair group, reading club or accessible sports session creates repeated contact between people who might otherwise remain strangers. This can build trust gradually and provide practical support. Such activities may be less visible than a major festival, yet their value should not be judged only by publicity or attendance on one day.

Funding decisions should therefore consider access, continuity and realistic staffing. A programme that depends on a few exhausted volunteers may not survive even if its initial event is popular. The council could support modest activities in existing buildings and review participation before expanding them. Larger events could still receive funding when their wider benefits are clearly explained and essential local services are protected.

In conclusion, a balanced cultural programme need not reject major occasions. Nevertheless, regular opportunities for residents to learn, meet and participate should form its foundation. Public money is more likely to create lasting value when success is defined through meaningful access and sustainable activity rather than a single impressive crowd.

tasks.title: Independent spoken response
tasks.instructions: Describe a time you helped someone learn a skill. Say who the person was, what they wanted to learn, what you did and how you felt. Prepare for one minute, then speak for up to two minutes.
tasks.model:
I helped a colleague, Leila, learn a new booking system at the community centre where we worked. She already knew how to welcome visitors and organise activities, but the software had changed and she was worried about making a reservation that nobody could find later.

We chose a quiet afternoon and used a practice account, so there was no risk of changing a real booking. I first asked her to create one reservation for a small meeting room. Rather than show every feature, I explained the three decisions she needed immediately: the date, the number of people and whether equipment was required. She entered the details while I watched.

When the confirmation appeared, it showed the following week instead of the intended date. I was tempted to correct it myself, but I asked her to compare the confirmation with her notes. She found the mistake and worked out which calendar control had caused it. We then changed the date and checked the confirmation again.

Before finishing, we practised a cancellation and wrote a short checklist in her own words. The next day she handled a visitor's request independently and only asked me to confirm one equipment option. I felt pleased because she had gained confidence through understanding the process, not through memorising where I clicked. Helping her also improved my own explanations. I learned that allowing someone time to notice and correct a small mistake can be more useful than giving a quick demonstration of everything.

A week later I asked which part still felt confusing. Leila said she could make ordinary bookings but wanted more practice with equipment requests. We arranged another short session rather than repeat the whole introduction. That follow-up mattered because her remaining question was specific, and it showed me that useful teaching continues after the first successful attempt.

data.objective: Exam-day planning and realistic practice
data.learn: Separate practical readiness from language performance. Use your own test-provider booking instructions to confirm identification, venue, delivery mode and arrival requirements. worked.example: My booking says to arrive at a specified time. I will confirm the venue entrance, check the journey beforehand and keep the provider’s contact details available. If transport fails, I will follow the provider’s instructions rather than assume a late arrival will be accepted.

tasks.title: Independent preparation plan
tasks.instructions: Write 100–160 words making a four-skill evidence review. For Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking, identify a task, a specific observed difficulty and a next action. Mark any skill not yet practised as unassessed. Distinguish checked answers from self-review and state how a fresh task or external feedback will test improvement.
tasks.model: In Listening, I confused a suggested time with the final arrangement; I will explain the contrast in a new conversation before checking its transcript. In Reading, I missed an exception in a workplace notice, so I will underline conditions in a fresh text and justify each answer. My letter addressed the problem but did not request a clear action. I will revise that paragraph, then write to a different recipient without the model. Speaking remains unassessed because I have not recorded a full long turn. I will prepare notes, record a response and ask a teacher for feedback on intelligibility. The checked-answer results show which local items I answered correctly; the writing and speaking plans do not establish a band. I will compare new evidence after these activities rather than rely on course completion alone.
rubric: Task achievement/response: I covered all letter points or developed every part of the essay question.
Coherence and cohesion: each paragraph develops a clear purpose, with logical links.
Lexical resource: register and collocations are natural and precise, rather than unnecessarily rare.
Grammatical range and accuracy: I checked tense, agreement and sentence boundaries in both simple and complex clauses.
tasks.analysis: Compare the message and reasoning, not just the vocabulary. Identify where the model addresses each instruction, how each paragraph develops its point, and one sentence you can improve in your own draft. This is an original teaching model, not an examiner-rated script.

tasks.title: Assessment reflection
tasks.instructions: Explain which skill currently has the weakest evidence in your four-skill review. Refer to a concrete task or an unassessed skill, propose a fresh follow-up and identify what requires human feedback.
tasks.model: My weakest evidence is in Speaking because checklist completion does not show whether another person understands my long turn. I can listen for obvious pauses and missing ideas, but a teacher may notice problems I overlook. I will record a new response on an unfamiliar topic, compare its development with my first attempt and request feedback on intelligibility. I will record that feedback separately from the platform’s completion credit.
rubric: Fluency and coherence: my ideas form a relevant, connected answer with useful development.
Lexical resource: I used natural, precise language and clarified meaning when needed.
Grammatical range and accuracy: I listened for tense, agreement and sentence control.
Pronunciation: I replayed the response and checked intelligibility, stress and meaningful pauses.
tasks.analysis: Replay your answer before comparing it with this possible response. Different relevant answers are valid. Record a second attempt to improve the specific issue you identified. A human partner or teacher is needed to evaluate live interaction reliably.

lesson.title: Reading: Read in Daily Life—Notices and Practical Conditions
lesson.subtitle: Extract a practical action from a notice

blocks.title: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Extract a practical action from a notice. Distinguish collection and return rules. Interpret conditions rather than assuming permission.

Read in Daily Life uses practical written material such as notices, messages and information displays. Read for who must do what, where and when. A notice may state different times for collection and return. A conditional renewal is not an automatic extension. Do not import rules from familiar institutions: the answer comes from this text. A strong paraphrase keeps both the action and its condition. Efficient reading means finding the relevant section, then reading closely enough to avoid exchanging one deadline for another. The short source here is original teaching material, not an ETS item.

blocks.title: Practical strategy
blocks.text: Identify purpose and audience. Mark actions, deadlines, exceptions and prohibited actions. For each question, locate the rule governing that exact stage rather than a nearby rule about a different stage.

Original daily-life notice: Equipment loans: Students may borrow a camera for up to three days. Collect reserved items between 12 and 2 pm at the media desk. Returns must be made in person before 4 pm on the due date. Do not place equipment in the book-return slot. For renewals, contact the desk before the due date; approval depends on other reservations.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: If a camera is due today, the borrower must return it in person before 4 pm. The 12–2 pm window applies to collecting reserved items, not returning them. A renewal request must be made before the due date and may be refused if another reservation exists.

Why it works: The answer keeps collection and return separate and preserves the conditional nature of renewal. It also respects the explicit prohibition on the book-return slot rather than assuming every borrowed item uses the same return process.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text: Do not treat “up to three days” as exactly three in every case, interpret a request as approved, or ignore the in-person return instruction.

blocks.title: Guided practice
blocks.text: A borrower wants to renew tomorrow when the item is due today. Explain the problem. Check: requests must be made before the due date, and approval is not guaranteed even when requested on time.

Independent practice: Find a real non-confidential public notice and write a plain-language action checklist for a specific user. Identify at least one condition and one potential confusion. Compare your checklist with the original wording to ensure it does not invent permission.

blocks.title: Recap
blocks.text: Practical reading connects the right action to the right time, location and condition.

data.objective: Reading: Read in Daily Life—Notices and Practical Conditions
data.learn: Read the source for its purpose, conditions and supporting evidence. In daily-life texts, track who must do what and in which order. In academic passages, distinguish observations, explanations and qualified conclusions. Use context to interpret vocabulary. These original shorter sets are non-adaptive skill practice, with local results rather than TOEFL score estimates.

A field-trip message

To: Environmental Science students
Subject: Friday’s estuary visit

The coach will leave from the north gate at 8:15. Please arrive ten minutes early because attendance must be checked before departure. The original meeting point outside the library is no longer in use due to roadworks.

Bring waterproof footwear, a packed lunch and the printed recording sheet. The department will provide sampling containers and gloves. Mobile coverage is unreliable at the estuary, so download the safety instructions before leaving campus.

Students who cannot walk the full route should contact the coordinator by Wednesday. A shorter accessible route can be arranged, but transport needs to be planned in advance. The visit will proceed in light rain. If severe weather requires cancellation, a message will be sent by 6:30 on Friday morning. Do not assume that ordinary rain means the trip is cancelled.

The arrangements should make the visit useful and safe, provided students read the updated instructions rather than relying on last term’s schedule.

lesson.title: Reading: Health Research, Comparisons and Causal Limits
lesson.subtitle: Interpret an outcome that combines actions

blocks.title: Learning objectives
blocks.text: Interpret an outcome that combines actions. Distinguish association from established causation. Read health-related prose using the evidence supplied.

Academic passages can discuss health without requiring specialist medical knowledge. Identify the groups, intervention, outcome and limitation. An outcome combining attendance or rescheduling differs from attendance alone. If group assignment was not random, a difference may reflect other group characteristics. The passage can support a promising association while withholding a causal conclusion. Do not import assumptions about treatment effectiveness or personal health decisions. This fictional example teaches research comprehension, not medical guidance. For TOEFL reading, the relevant skill is understanding what the author claims and why a limitation is introduced.

blocks.title: Practical strategy
blocks.text: Make a compact comparison: message A, message B, measured outcome, uncertainty. For each option, check whether it preserves the combined outcome and the strength of the conclusion.

Original fictional academic passage: Researchers compared two reminder messages for voluntary campus health appointments. One gave only the appointment date; the other included the date and a link to change the booking. More recipients of the second message attended or rescheduled. Because participants were not randomly assigned, the report cautions that other differences between the groups may have affected the result. It recommends a randomised follow-up rather than claiming that the link alone caused the improvement.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Supported summary: “Including a change-booking link was associated with more attendance or rescheduling, but the non-random groups prevent a firm causal conclusion.” Unsupported summary: “The link proved a health treatment works.” No treatment was tested, and the outcome was booking behaviour.

Why it works: The supported version names the actual difference and outcome while retaining the author’s limitation. The unsupported version changes both the intervention and the certainty of the evidence.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text: Do not read attended or rescheduled as attended only, assume equal groups without evidence, or infer a medical benefit from an appointment-booking outcome.

blocks.title: Guided practice
blocks.text: Explain why a randomised follow-up is recommended. Check: it would help address the possibility that pre-existing group differences affected results. It would not by itself turn booking behaviour into a treatment outcome.

Independent practice: Write three questions about the passage: one detail, one purpose and one inference. Supply a source-based explanation for each. Make one distractor that changes the outcome and another that exaggerates certainty, then explain why both fail.

blocks.title: Recap
blocks.text: Read the measured outcome and the stated limits precisely; promising association is not automatically established causation.

tasks.title: Independent passage: Reading: Health Research, Comparisons and Causal Limits
tasks.instructions: Read the complete source and answer each question. Use only the evidence given. These are original lesson tasks, not a complete examination paper.
tasks.source:
When a health average hides variation

An average can summarise a health outcome, but it may conceal important differences among participants. Suppose a programme produces a modest average improvement while helping one group substantially and making little difference to another. Reporting only the overall figure would not show who benefited or why.

Researchers therefore examine variation, while avoiding the temptation to explain every subgroup difference after seeing the results. Dividing a small sample into many categories can produce apparent patterns by chance. A useful analysis distinguishes questions planned in advance from exploratory observations that need confirmation.

The way an outcome is measured matters too. A self-reported improvement in comfort is valuable, but it is not identical to a change in physical function. Neither measure should automatically replace the other. Together, they may provide a fuller account of what participants experience.

The writer argues for reporting benefits with enough detail to reveal uncertainty and practical meaning. This does not make an intervention ineffective simply because its effects vary. It helps readers understand which claims are supported and what further research should investigate.

questions.evidence: Apparent patterns may arise by chance.
questions.explanation: The source supports this answer: Apparent patterns may arise by chance.

questions.prompt: How does the writer recommend interpreting health benefits?
answers: Averages need context about variation, measurement and uncertainty.
questions.evidence: The writer argues for reporting benefits with enough detail to reveal uncertainty and practical meaning. This does not make an intervention ineffective simply because its effects vary. It helps readers understand which claims are supported and what further research should investigate.
questions.explanation: Averages need context about variation, measurement and uncertainty. Compare the conditions and scope in the passage: the other options remove a stated restriction, confuse measures, or claim more than the evidence establishes.
options: The overall average describes every participant equally well.

lesson.title: Exam-day planning and realistic practice
lesson.subtitle: IELTS General Training: learn, practise, review and improve

blocks.title: What you will learn
blocks.text:
Separate confirmed booking requirements from assumptions.
Construct a realistic contingency plan and communicate what still needs checking.

blocks.title: Before you begin
blocks.text: This module concerns logistical preparation, not a language score. Test-provider instructions govern identification, arrival, venue and delivery details for a particular booking. The course should not invent those requirements for you.

blocks.title: Use three evidence categories
blocks.text: Confirmed means a requirement is explicitly stated in the relevant booking or provider guidance. To verify means a detail remains unclear or absent. Personal plan means an action you choose, such as checking a route or packing permitted items. Mixing these categories can turn sensible advice into a false official rule.

Example: ‘My booking gives an arrival time’ is confirmed only if you actually have that instruction. ‘I will check the entrance before travelling’ is a personal action. ‘I need to confirm whether my identification matches the booking requirements’ is an unresolved check. If you have no booking, label the entire scenario hypothetical instead of inventing a document.

blocks.title: Build a contingency with a trigger and action
blocks.text: A contingency is not a promise that a problem cannot happen. It connects a trigger to a response: if the first train is cancelled, check the planned alternative and follow the provider’s contact instructions where necessary. A travel buffer is your planning choice; it does not override a stated latest arrival time or guarantee acceptance if late.

Worked record: requirement source—booking email; known detail—specified venue and arrival instruction; personal action—check travel and entrance; unresolved detail—delivery-specific permitted items; contingency—use an alternative route and consult the provider if disruption affects arrival. The record keeps source and assumption visible.

blocks.title: Plan the final preparation realistically
blocks.text: Choose a limited revision task that does not depend on learning an entire new system at the last moment. For example, review one evidence-tracking error and the location of essential booking information. A long checklist that cannot be completed may increase confusion rather than readiness.

In the writing and spoken reflection, explain why each step exists. ‘Check the route’ becomes more useful when linked to an unfamiliar entrance or a known transfer. Avoid prescribing universal identification documents, arrival minutes or test-centre rules. Those are booking-specific facts that must be verified from the actual provider.

blocks.title: Pause and apply
blocks.text: Why is ‘I will arrive early, therefore the provider must admit me’ an unsupported conclusion?

blocks.title: Compare your reasoning
blocks.text: A personal plan does not determine the provider’s admission rules or whether other requirements are met. State the plan separately and verify the applicable booking conditions.

blocks.title: Apply this in the practice lab
blocks.text: The guided task separates confirmed and unknown details. The independent final-day plan adds a travel contingency and preparation limit. The spoken assessment explains a disruption response while identifying what still needs verification. None of these outcomes establishes an examination band.

activity.prompt: Exam-day planning and realistic practice — guided practice, independent response and transfer assessment

data.objective: Exam-day planning and realistic practice
data.learn: Separate practical readiness from language performance. Use your own test-provider booking instructions to confirm identification, venue, delivery mode and arrival requirements. Mark unknown details for verification rather than inventing rules. Plan travel, a backup route and a realistic final-day routine. This logistical plan is not evidence of an IELTS band; the next module reviews language-learning evidence across four skills.

worked.example: My booking says to arrive at a specified time. I will confirm the venue entrance, check the journey beforehand and keep the provider’s contact details available. If transport fails, I will follow the provider’s instructions rather than assume a late arrival will be accepted.
worked.reasoning: The plan separates a verified requirement, an action and a contingency. Local advice cannot replace the instructions for a particular booking.

tasks.title: Guided logistics check
tasks.instructions: Write 60–90 words distinguishing two details confirmed in your booking instructions from two details you still need to check. If you have no booking, use a clearly labelled hypothetical checklist. Do not invent identification or arrival rules.
tasks.model: I have not booked a test yet, so this is a hypothetical checklist rather than a statement of test-provider rules. I would first confirm the exact venue and the identification document required for my booking. I would also check the stated arrival time and whether the Speaking appointment is separate. Until I receive those instructions, I should not assume that another candidate’s arrangements apply to me.
rubric: I distinguish confirmed instructions from assumptions.
I identify a reliable source for details still to verify.
My actions and contingency are specific and feasible.
My wording is clear and does not invent test-provider rules.
tasks.analysis: Check that the plan distinguishes verified instructions, personal choices, unknown details and contingencies. This is logistics self-review, not assessment of examination readiness.

tasks.title: Independent final-day plan
tasks.instructions: Write 100–140 words planning the day before and the morning of your test. Include the source of requirements, a travel contingency, and a realistic preparation limit. Separate confirmed information from details still to verify.
tasks.model: The day before my test, I would read the latest booking instructions and check the venue entrance against a map. I would prepare the identification specified by the provider and keep the booking details available. I would check the route and identify another way to travel if the usual service were disrupted. The departure time would depend on the required arrival time, which I still need to confirm. I would finish heavy practice early enough to rest, rather than attempt to learn a new essay script late at night. In the morning, I would check for messages from the provider and follow its instructions if a practical problem arose.
rubric: I distinguish confirmed instructions from assumptions.
I identify a reliable source for details still to verify.
My actions and contingency are specific and feasible.
My wording is clear and does not invent test-provider rules.
tasks.analysis: Check that the plan distinguishes verified instructions, personal choices, unknown details and contingencies. This is logistics self-review, not assessment of examination readiness.

tasks.title: Assessment: explain a contingency
tasks.instructions: Explain how you would handle a transport disruption on test day. Distinguish your own backup plan from the test provider’s rules; identify one detail you must verify.
tasks.model: I would first check whether my planned alternative route could still reach the venue in time. I would keep the provider’s contact information available and follow its instructions if arrival became uncertain. I would not assume that sending a message automatically permits late entry. Before test day, I need to verify the required arrival time and the procedure for reporting a serious disruption.
rubric: Fluency and coherence: my ideas form a relevant, connected answer with useful development.
Lexical resource: I used natural, precise language and clarified meaning when needed.
Grammatical range and accuracy: I listened for tense, agreement and sentence control.
Pronunciation: I replayed the response and checked intelligibility, stress and meaningful pauses.
tasks.analysis: Check that the plan distinguishes verified instructions, personal choices, unknown details and contingencies. This is logistics self-review, not assessment of examination readiness.
